mainTopic: The flame blessing at הבדלה, returning to bentch, the time limit for ברכת המזון, answering אמן, and washing and oil before ברכת המזון
overview: This amud finishes פרק אלו דברים. It first explains the משנה's rule that one blesses over the הבדלה flame only when one can benefit from its light. רב says potential benefit is enough, even from a distance, and the גמרא defends him against a ברייתא by explaining that 'seeing without using' means a fading flame. A ברייתא then rules that glowing coals qualify but dimming coals, עוממות, do not. רבא disagrees with רב and requires actual benefit, measured by telling coins or weights apart. Each אמורא acted on his own view, and we learn that one need not search for a flame. Next the גמרא limits the dispute about returning to bentch to someone who forgot, and adds stories of reward for going back. It then sets the time limit for bentching by digestion and discusses answering אמן, including whether blessing or answering is greater and whether to answer schoolchildren. The chapter closes with oil and washing the hands before ברכת המזון.

steps.title: The משנה: No blessing over the candle until one benefits from it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line from the משנה that one does not bless over the flame until one can benefit from its light.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one does not recite the blessing over the candle until one benefits from its light.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה so it can explain it next. This sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key word is יאותו, meaning 'they will benefit' from the light. The question the גמרא will ask is how much benefit is needed. Must you actually use the light, or is it enough that you could?

keyTerms.meaning: Candle or flame (here, the הבדלה flame)

phrases.english: And one does not recite a blessing over the candle
phrases.notes: Refers to the blessing בורא מאורי האש said at הבדלה.

phrases.english: until they benefit from its light.
phrases.notes: The word יאותו is what רב will explain next.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין מְבָרְכִין עַל הַנֵּר עַד שֶׁיֵּאוֹתוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening quote of the משנה for this sugya.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The blessing over the flame requires benefit from its light.

steps.title: רב: Potential benefit is enough, even from a distance
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב explains that 'benefit' does not mean actually using the light. It is enough that one could use it if one stood close, even if one is now far away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: 'They benefit' does not mean actual benefit. Rather, it is enough that if one stood close, one could use its light. This is true even if one is now at a distance.
steps.whatsHappening: רב explains the משנה's word יאותו in a lenient way. You do not need to actually use the light. The flame only needs to be the kind that gives usable light.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב changes the requirement from 'actual use' to 'usable light.' So a person standing far away may still bless if he sees the flame, because someone nearby could use its light. This creates the position that the גמרא will soon challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: Distance of place, i.e., standing far away

steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying you may bless over a flame that gives no usable light at all. He means the light must be usable for someone standing near it, even if you yourself are far away.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
phrases.notes: This just tells us who is speaking; his words follow right after.

phrases.english: 'They benefit' does not mean they actually benefit,
rather, any case where, if he stood close by,
he could use its light,
phrases.notes: This is potential use, not actual use.

phrases.english: even if he is now at a distance.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: לֹא יֵאוֹתוּ יֵאוֹתוּ מַמָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the key word יאותו from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Potential benefit is enough. One may bless over a flame seen from a distance if its light would be usable up close.

steps.title: רב אשי agrees: The משנה includes a distant viewer
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the same thing: the משנה's rule applies even to someone standing far away.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so too, רב אשי said: We learned this ruling even for one at a distance.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא, רב אשי, backs up רב's reading. He confirms that the משנה's rule also covers someone standing far from the flame.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds no new rule. It shows that רב's lenient reading had support among later sages as well. That makes the challenge that follows more serious, since it targets both of them.

keyTerms.meaning: And so too (introduces an agreeing opinion)

phrases.english: And so too, Rav Ashi said:
We learned this even for one at a distance.
phrases.notes: The משנה's permission applies even when standing far away.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: בְּרִיחוּק מָקוֹם שָׁנִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: An agreeing opinion that supports רב's reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's rule applies even at a distance, in agreement with רב.

steps.title: A ברייתא requires both seeing the flame and using its light
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא listing cases where one may not bless: a hidden candle, a candle inside a lantern, seeing without using, and using without seeing. One must both see the flame and use its light.
steps.simpleTranslation: They objected: If he had a candle hidden in his lap or inside a lantern, or he saw the flame but did not use its light, or he used its light but did not see the flame, he does not bless until he both sees the flame and uses its light.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to contradict רב. This step only quotes the source. The next step shows exactly where it clashes with רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא sets two conditions: seeing the flame and using its light. The phrase 'he saw the flame but did not use its light' is the danger for רב. If a distant viewer counts as 'not using,' then the ברייתא forbids exactly what רב allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: His lap, or the fold of his garment
Lantern (here, one that hides the flame)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
phrases.notes: Signals a challenge from a ברייתא.

phrases.english: If he had a candle hidden in his lap,
or inside a lantern,
phrases.notes: The flame cannot be seen.

phrases.english: or if he saw a flame
but did not use its light,
phrases.notes: This case becomes the basis of the challenge.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ נִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ לְאוֹרָהּ וְלֹא רָאָה שַׁלְהֶבֶת —
phrases.english: or he used its light but did not see the flame —
he does not bless until he sees the flame
and uses its light.
phrases.notes: Both conditions are required.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: הָיְתָה לוֹ נֵר טְמוּנָה בְּחֵיקוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא to challenge רב and רב אשי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling (and רב אשי's) that one may bless from a distance.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא requires actually using the light, not just seeing the flame. That seems to rule out a distant viewer.

steps.title: How can one see a flame without using it? Only from far away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the ברייתא's cases. Using the light without seeing the flame happens when the flame is around a corner. But seeing the flame without using its light must mean standing far away. So distance disqualifies, which contradicts רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, using its light without seeing the flame can happen when the flame is around a corner. But how can seeing the flame without using its light happen? Is it not when one is far away?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the ברייתא's case of 'seeing but not using' could happen. The implied answer is that the person is far away. This finishes the challenge: the ברייתא forbids blessing from a distance, against רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'around a corner' case is easy to picture: the light spills out, but the flame is hidden. For 'saw but did not use,' the only obvious case is distance. So the ברייתא seems to say a distant viewer may not bless, directly against רב and רב אשי.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted; this part is understandable (sets up a contrast)
You can find it (a realistic case)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as a simple question looking for information. The question 'how can this happen?' is the heart of the attack, since its only obvious answer is 'from a distance.'
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next move. The גמרא will need to find another way to picture 'seeing without using,' so that רב's ruling allowing blessing from a distance can stand.

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁלָמָא מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ לְאוֹרָהּ וְלֹא רָאָה שַׁלְהֶבֶת
phrases.english: Granted, using its light but not seeing the flame
you can find such a case —
where the flame stands around a corner.
phrases.notes: The light reaches him, but the flame is out of sight.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא רָאָה שַׁלְהֶבֶת וְלֹא נִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ לְאוֹרָהּ
phrases.english: But seeing the flame without using its light,
how can you find such a case?
Is it not where it is far away?!
phrases.notes: Rhetorical: implies distance disqualifies, against רב.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ לְאוֹרָהּ וְלֹא רָאָה שַׁלְהֶבֶת מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Works out the cases in the ברייתא to sharpen the challenge against רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's permission to bless from a distance.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The only realistic way to see a flame without using it is distance. The ברייתא forbids that, so distance should disqualify.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What realistic case fits the ברייתא's 'saw the flame but did not use its light'?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Implied: a distant viewer, which would contradict רב. The גמרא's real answer comes next.

steps.title: Seeing without using means a fading flame, not distance
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the claim that the ברייתא's 'seeing without using' must mean standing far away. It can mean a flame that is slowly dying out.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. The case is a flame that is gradually dimming.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge against רב. 'Seeing the flame but not using its light' does not have to mean being far away. It can mean the flame itself is dying out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed the only way to see a flame without using its light is distance. The גמרא offers another case: the flame is so weak that its light cannot be used by anyone, near or far. So the ברייתא never ruled against distance, and רב's rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: That keeps getting dimmer and dimmer

steps.whatToRemember: רב's rule survives. The ברייתא's 'sees but does not use' is about a fading flame. Distance is not the problem as long as one could use the light if one stood close.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two problems. Distance is about where the person stands, and that is fine. A fading flame is about the fire itself being too weak, and that is not fine.

phrases.english: No,
phrases.notes: The answer: the case doesn't have to be about distance.

phrases.english: the case is one where it keeps dimming.
phrases.notes: The flame is fading, so its light is useless even up close.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, כְּגוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 5 by reinterpreting the ברייתא's case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the case (אוקימתא): the case is a dying flame, not distance.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Seeing without using can only mean standing far away, so distance disqualifies.
steps.terutzMaskana: Seeing without using means a flame too weak to give useful light. Distance alone does not disqualify, which fits רב.

steps.title: Glowing coals qualify for the blessing, dying coals do not
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that one may bless over glowing coals but not over coals that are dying out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: Over glowing coals, one blesses. Over dimming coals, one does not bless.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about whether coals can be used for the fire blessing. It starts a new topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This builds on the same idea as the fading flame. Fire counts only when it is truly alive and gives off real light. Glowing coals still have living fire, but dimming coals are on their way out.

keyTerms.meaning: Glowing, smoldering coals that are still alive

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Glowing coals: one blesses over them,
dimming ones: one does not bless over them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a related new topic. It moves from candles to coals, with the same theme of fading fire.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Glowing coals may be used for the fire blessing. Dimming coals may not.

steps.title: What counts as glowing coals?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how to define 'glowing' coals.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case of glowing coals?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a clear definition of 'glowing' coals. This sets up רב חסדא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא drew a line between glowing and dimming coals but did not say where the line is. The גמרא wants a practical test.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How do we picture it?

phrases.english: What is the case of glowing coals?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a definition of a term in the ברייתא from Step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical test for when coals count as 'glowing'.

steps.title: The wood chip test
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says coals are 'glowing' if a wood chip put among them catches fire by itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Any coals where, if one puts a wood chip in among them, it catches fire on its own.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives a simple test. If a small chip of wood bursts into flame by itself when placed in the coals, the coals are 'glowing' and one may bless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test measures whether the coals still have real fire inside them. If you have to blow on them to light the chip, they are too weak and count as dimming.

keyTerms.meaning: It ignites by itself, without blowing

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
Any coals where, if one puts a wood chip into them,
it ignites on its own.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of Step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Coals are glowing if a wood chip placed among them ignites by itself.

steps.title: Is the word spelled with an א or an ע?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the ברייתא's word for 'dimming' is אוממות (with an א) or עוממות (with an ע).
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: Is it 'אוממות' with an א or 'עוממות' with an ע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about the exact text of the ברייתא. Which letter does the word for 'dimming' start with? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a question about the correct reading of the word, not about the law. The ruling stays the same either way, and the גמרא simply wants the right version of the text.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among the scholars

steps.confusionAlert: Do not look for a practical difference here. The law is the same either way. This is only about the correct spelling and reading.

phrases.english: It was asked of them:
Is it 'omemot' with an alef, or 'omemot' with an ayin?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא of Step 7 to ask about its exact wording.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The correct spelling of the word for 'dimming' coals: with an א or an ע.

steps.title: A פסוק shows the word is spelled with an ע
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא בר אבדימי brings a פסוק in יחזקאל that uses the root עמם (with an ע) to mean 'dim'. So the correct reading is עוממות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as רב חסדא בר אבדימי said: 'The cedars in the garden of God could not dim it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the spelling question with a פסוק. The word עממהו, meaning 'dimmed it', is spelled with an ע, so the ברייתא's word is עוממות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק shows that the root meaning 'to dim' or 'to overshadow' is spelled with an ע in תנ״ך. That settles which letter belongs in the ברייתא's word.

keyTerms.meaning: Dimmed it, overshadowed it (spelled with an ע)

steps.whatToRemember: Glowing coals pass the wood chip test and may be used for the blessing. Dimming coals, עוממות spelled with an ע, may not.

phrases.english: Come and hear,
for Rav Chisda bar Avdimi said:
'The cedars in the garden of God could not dim it.'
phrases.notes: יחזקאל לא:ח. The root עמם, meaning dim, is spelled with an ע.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע דְּאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא בַּר אַבְדִּימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the spelling question from Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word is עוממות, with an ע, as shown by the word עממהו in the פסוק.

steps.title: רבא: you must actually benefit from the light
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the משנה's word יֵאוֹתוּ means you must truly benefit from the candle's light.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: 'Benefit' means actually benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's word יֵאוֹתוּ ('they benefit'). רבא says it means exactly what it says: you must really use the light.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the sugya, רב יהודה in the name of רב read the word loosely: you only need to be close enough that you could benefit. רבא disagrees and reads it literally, so you must actually be close enough to use the light. This raises the obvious next question: how close is that?

keyTerms.meaning: 'They benefit' — the משנה's word for getting use from the light

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not follow from the coals discussion right before it (steps 7-11). It goes back to the earlier argument about the משנה's word יֵאוֹתוּ.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
'They benefit' — actually.
phrases.notes: The benefit must be real, not just possible.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרָבָא אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the coals discussion and returns to the earlier argument about what יֵאוֹתוּ means. It gives the literal view, against רב יהודה's loose reading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: To bless on a flame, you must actually be able to use its light.

steps.title: How close counts as benefiting?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how much benefit, meaning how close to the light, is required.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much?
steps.whatsHappening: Following רבא's view, the גמרא asks for a measure: how close must you be to count as benefiting? This question sets up the answers in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once benefit must be real, we need a clear test for it. The question asks for a practical standard, not a reason.

keyTerms.meaning: And how much? — a request for a measure

phrases.english: And how much?
phrases.notes: How close or how much light is needed?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכַמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a measure of the real benefit that רבא requires.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How close to the flame you must be for it to count as benefiting from its light.

steps.title: עולא: close enough to tell two coins apart
steps.stepSummary: עולא says you must be close enough to tell an איסר from a פונדיון.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: close enough that you can tell the difference between an איסר coin and a פונדיון coin.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא gives the first test. If the light lets you tell two similar coins apart, you are benefiting from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An איסר and a פונדיון were coins that looked fairly alike. Telling them apart needs enough light to see fine details, so that is the proof of real use.

keyTerms.meaning: That he can recognize or tell apart

phrases.english: Ulla said:
Enough that he can tell an issar from a pundeyon.
phrases.notes: Two coins of that time.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּכִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question 'how much?'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Enough light to tell an איסר from a פונדיון.

steps.title: חזקיה: close enough to tell two city weights apart
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה says you must be close enough to tell the weight used in טבריה from the one used in ציפורי.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said: close enough that you can tell the difference between a weight from טבריה and a weight from ציפורי.
steps.whatsHappening: חזקיה gives a second answer to the same question. He uses two weights from two cities as his test.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The weights of the two cities were only slightly different, so telling them apart also needs clear light. חזקיה picks a different everyday object to measure the same idea: enough light to see small differences.

keyTerms.meaning: A weight or stamp (meaning not certain)

phrases.english: Hizkiya said:

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּכִּיר בֵּין מְלוּזְמָא שֶׁל טְבֶרְיָא
phrases.english: Enough that he can tell a weight of Tiberias
from a weight of Tzippori.
phrases.notes: The two were only slightly different.

steps.triggerLanguage: חִזְקִיָּה אָמַר כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּכִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the same question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Enough light to tell the weight of טבריה from the weight of ציפורי.

steps.title: How the אמוראים actually blessed on light
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה blessed on light from a far house, רבא on light from a nearby house, and אביי on light from בר אבוה's house.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה would bless on the light of the house of אדא the servant. רבא would bless on the light of the house of גוריא בר חמא. אביי would bless on the light of the house of בר אבוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells what each אמורא did at the end of שבת. Each one acted on his own view about how close to the light you must be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה held you only need to be able to benefit, so he blessed even on a far light (אדא's house). רבא held you must actually benefit, so he blessed on a light right next door (גוריא בר חמא's house). Their actions match the views they stated.

keyTerms.meaning: On the house of — on the light coming from that house

phrases.aramaic: רַב יְהוּדָה מְבָרֵךְ אַדְּבֵי אַדָּא דַּיָּילָא,
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda would bless on the house of Adda the servant,
phrases.notes: A house far away.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא מְבָרֵךְ אַדְּבֵי גּוּרְיָא בַּר חָמָא.
phrases.english: Rava would bless on the house of Gurya bar Hama.
phrases.notes: A house right next to his.

phrases.english: Abaye would bless on the house of bar Avuh.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יְהוּדָה מְבָרֵךְ אַדְּבֵי אַדָּא דַּיָּילָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the two views about benefiting from light carried out in real life.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each אמורא's practice matched his view on how close you must be to the light.

steps.title: No need to chase after a flame
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב rules that you do not need to go looking for a flame the way you go looking for other מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: We do not chase after fire the way we chase after מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: A new rule is given. If you have no flame at the end of שבת, you do not have to go searching for one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally we make an effort to find and do מצוות. The ברכה on fire is different: you say it if a flame is there, but you do not have to search for one. Without a flame you can still make הבדלה.

keyTerms.meaning: We go around looking for, chase after

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical הלכה: missing a flame does not stop your הבדלה, and you do not have to go out of your way to find one.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
We do not go seeking after the flame
the way one seeks after מצוות.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב אֵין מְחַזְּרִין עַל הָאוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how close you must be to a new question: whether you must search for a flame at all.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You do not have to go looking for a flame for the ברכה at הבדלה.

steps.title: רבי זירא changed his practice
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא used to search for a flame. After hearing רב's rule he stopped, but he still blesses if a flame happens to be there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: At first I used to go looking for a flame. Once I heard what רב יהודה said in the name of רב, I also stopped looking. But if a flame happens to come my way, I bless on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא tells how he changed what he did after hearing רב's rule. His story shows how the rule works in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before hearing the rule, he treated the flame like any מצוה and went looking for it. After hearing it, he stopped searching. But the ברכה still has value, so when a flame is right there he says it.

keyTerms.meaning: It happens to come to me

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ideas here. First, how close to the flame: רב יהודה says close enough that you could benefit, while רבא says you must actually benefit (tested by telling coins or weights apart). Second, you do not have to search for a flame, but if one is right there, you bless on it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
At first I used to seek out the flame,
once I heard this
that Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav,
I too do not seek it out,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִי מִקְּלַע לִי מִמֵּילָא — מְבָרֵיכְנָא.
phrases.english: but if one comes to me on its own — I bless.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא מֵרֵישׁ הֲוָה מְהַדַּרְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows רב's rule being accepted and put into practice, and adds that you still bless when a flame is available.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: You do not search for a flame for הבדלה, but if one is there, you bless on it.

steps.title: The dispute is only when he forgot, not when he skipped on purpose
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד (or רב דימי בר אבא) limits the משנה's dispute to someone who forgot. If he skipped bentching on purpose (במזיד), everyone agrees he must go back to where he ate.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the משנה's case of 'one who ate and forgot': רב זביד said, and some say it was רב דימי בר אבא: The argument is only when he forgot. If he did it on purpose, everyone agrees he must go back to his place and bentch.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the opening words of the משנה and brings an אמורא who limits the dispute to a case where the person forgot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, בית שמאי say he goes back to where he ate, and בית הלל say he bentches wherever he remembers. רב זביד adds that בית הלל's leniency covers only someone who forgot. A person who skipped the ברכה on purpose gets no leniency, and even בית הלל require him to return.

phrases.english: 'One who ate,' etc.
phrases.notes: The opening words of the משנה: one who ate and forgot to bentch.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב דִּימִי בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Zevid said, and some say Rav Dimi bar Abba said:
The dispute is in a case where he forgot,
but if he did it on purpose, everyone agrees:
he must return to his place and bless.
phrases.notes: His place means the place where he ate.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב דִּימִי בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic. It moves from the ברכה on fire (נר) to the משנה about forgetting ברכת המזון.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dispute between בית שמאי and בית הלל applies only to someone who forgot. Someone who skipped bentching on purpose must return to the place where he ate, according to everyone.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious? The משנה says 'forgot'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב זביד: the משנה already says 'and forgot,' so why do we need him to tell us the dispute is only about forgetting?
steps.simpleTranslation: It's obvious! We learned in the משנה 'and he forgot.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב זביד's statement is needed at all, since the משנה's own wording already describes a person who forgot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה explicitly describes a person who forgot. So limiting the dispute to forgetting seems to add nothing new. This is a פשיטא challenge: it attacks the statement as unnecessary, not as wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (a challenge that a statement adds nothing new)

steps.confusionAlert: פשיטא does not mean רב זביד is wrong. It means his point seems too obvious to need saying.

phrases.english: It's obvious!
'And he forgot' is what we learned in the Mishnah.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רב זביד's statement in Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב זביד's statement that the dispute is limited to someone who forgot
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'forgot' in the משנה already makes this clear, so the statement seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Without רב זביד, we might think 'forgot' was there to show how strict בית שמאי are
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that we might have thought בית הלל are lenient even for someone who skipped on purpose. On that reading, the word 'forgot' would only be there to show that בית שמאי are strict even in the mild case. רב זביד teaches that this is not so.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said that the same law (בית הלל's leniency) applies even to someone who skipped on purpose. On that view, the משנה said 'forgot' only to show you how far בית שמאי go. So רב זביד teaches us that this is not the case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'it's obvious' challenge. It shows that the word 'forgot' could have been read differently, so רב זביד's statement is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'forgot' could have been a way of showing the strength of בית שמאי's view: even someone who merely forgot must go back. If so, בית הלל would let even someone who skipped on purpose bentch wherever he is. רב זביד rules this reading out, so the deliberate case is required to return according to everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (introduces a mistaken assumption we could have had)
To let you know their strength (how far their view goes)
He teaches us (that the mistaken assumption is wrong)

steps.whatToRemember: Whether a person forgot or skipped on purpose matters. בית הלל's leniency is only for someone who forgot. Someone who skipped bentching on purpose must go back, according to everyone.

phrases.english: You might have said
that the same law applies even when he did it on purpose,
phrases.notes: That is, בית הלל would allow bentching in place even for the deliberate case.

phrases.english: and the reason it teaches 'and he forgot'
is to let you know the strength of Beit Shammai's view.
phrases.notes: בית שמאי require going back even for someone who merely forgot.

phrases.english: So he teaches us that this is not so.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְתֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of Step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: shows a plausible mistaken reading that the statement comes to rule out
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'forgot' was only there to show how strict בית שמאי are, so בית הלל would be lenient even for someone who skipped on purpose.
steps.terutzMaskana: בית הלל are lenient only for someone who forgot. Someone who skipped on purpose must return, according to everyone.

steps.title: בית הלל challenge בית שמאי: must he climb all the way back up?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records בית הלל arguing against בית שמאי. If someone ate at the top of the בירה, forgot, and came down without bentching, does he really have to climb all the way back up to bentch?
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: בית הלל said to בית שמאי: According to you, someone who ate at the top of the בירה, forgot, came down, and did not bentch must go back up to the top of the בירה and bentch?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with the actual debate. Here בית הלל attack בית שמאי's view by pointing to a case where it seems too demanding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית הלל pick a dramatic case: the place he ate is high up and hard to get back to. Requiring a long climb just to bentch seems unreasonable. They use this to show that בית שמאי's rule goes too far.

keyTerms.meaning: The top of the בירה (a high place; a tall fortress or the Temple Mount)

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמְרוּ לָהֶם בֵּית הִלֵּל לְבֵית שַׁמַּאי:
phrases.english: It was taught: Beit Hillel said to Beit Shammai:
According to your words, one who ate at the top of the Bira
phrases.notes: Some explain הבירה as the Temple Mount, others as a tall fortress. Either way, it's a high place that's hard to get back to.

phrases.english: and forgot, and went down, and did not bless,
must he go back to the top of the Bira and bless?!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question that shows how hard this would be.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמְרוּ לָהֶם בֵּית הִלֵּל לְבֵית שַׁמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the ברייתא that records the reasoning behind the משנה's dispute.
steps.kashyaTarget: בית שמאי's ruling that one must return to the place where he ate
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule would demand an unreasonable effort, such as climbing back up a high place just to bentch.

steps.title: בית שמאי answer: you would climb back for your wallet, so surely for Heaven's honor
steps.stepSummary: בית שמאי reply with a קל וחומר. A person would climb back up to get a wallet he forgot there. If he climbs for his own needs, surely he should climb for the honor of Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: בית שמאי said to בית הלל: According to you, someone who forgot his wallet at the top of the בירה would not go up and get it? He goes up for his own honor (his own needs), so for the honor of Heaven, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: בית שמאי answer בית הלל's challenge. They argue that the climb is not unreasonable, because people make that same effort for their own belongings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בית הלל said the climb was too much effort. בית שמאי show that people gladly make that effort for a lost wallet. Using a קל וחומר, they argue that a ברכה, which is for the honor of Heaven, deserves at least as much effort as personal property.

keyTerms.meaning: For his own honor (his own needs)
All the more so (the closing words of a קל וחומר)

steps.whatToRemember: בית שמאי's reasoning: if you would go back for your wallet, you should go back to bentch. Remember that the משנה's dispute covers only someone who forgot.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that בית שמאי's view is based on treating a מצוה with at least as much seriousness as one's own property.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן בֵּית שַׁמַּאי לְבֵית הִלֵּל:
phrases.english: Beit Shammai said to Beit Hillel:

phrases.aramaic: לְדִבְרֵיכֶם מִי שֶׁשָּׁכַח אַרְנָקִי בְּרֹאשׁ הַבִּירָה
phrases.english: According to your words, one who forgot his wallet at the top of the Bira
would he not go up and take it?
phrases.notes: Of course he would.

phrases.english: For his own honor he goes up,
for the honor of Heaven, all the more so!
phrases.notes: This completes the קל וחומר.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן בֵּית שַׁמַּאי לְבֵית הִלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends בית שמאי against בית הלל's challenge in Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: קל וחומר: compares the effort to what people already do for their own property
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Climbing back up to bentch is too much effort to require.
steps.terutzMaskana: People make the same effort for a wallet, so the honor of Heaven surely justifies it.

steps.title: Two students: one rewarded, one punished
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tells a story about two students who left without bentching. The one who had forgotten went back like בית שמאי and found a purse of gold. The one who skipped on purpose and relied on בית הלל was eaten by a lion.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were two students. One had forgotten, followed בית שמאי by going back, and found a gold purse. The other skipped bentching on purpose, followed בית הלל by not going back, and a lion ate him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story to show the real-life results of going back to bentch where you ate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second student skipped on purpose (מזיד). According to רב זביד in Step 19, even בית הלל agree that in that case you must go back. So he wrongly relied on בית הלל's leniency in a case where it does not apply, and he was punished. The first student went back even though he had only forgotten, and he was rewarded.

keyTerms.meaning: by mistake, without meaning to (here: he forgot)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this story as saying בית הלל are wrong. The second student did something on purpose. In that case even בית הלל require going back (Step 19). His mistake was relying on בית הלל where they do not actually rule leniently.

phrases.english: There were these two students [who ate and did not bentch].
One did it by mistake, and acted like Beit Shammai [and went back]
phrases.notes: He forgot, yet still went back to where he ate.

phrases.english: and he found a purse of gold.
And one did it on purpose, and acted like Beit Hillel [and did not go back]
phrases.notes: He relied on בית הלל, even though they agree that one who skipped on purpose must go back.

phrases.english: and a lion ate him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ תְּרֵי תַּלְמִידֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Right after בית שמאי's קל וחומר about climbing back for the honor of Heaven, the גמרא shows in a story that going back brings reward.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Going back to bentch where one ate is rewarded. Wrongly relying on a leniency when one skipped on purpose brings punishment.

steps.title: רבה בר בר חנה and the golden dove
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה forgot to bentch while traveling with a caravan. He did not want the caravan to tell him to just bentch where he was. So he told them he had forgotten a golden dove. He went back, bentched, and actually found a golden dove.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה was traveling with a caravan. He ate, forgot, and did not bentch. He thought: 'If I tell them I forgot to bentch, they will say: bentch here, since wherever you bentch you are blessing God. Better to tell them I forgot a golden dove.' So he said, 'Wait for me, I forgot a golden dove.' He went back, bentched, and found a golden dove.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about a great אמורא who went back to bentch where he ate, and he was rewarded.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר בר חנה had only forgotten, so by בית הלל he could have bentched where he was. Still, he wanted to be strict like בית שמאי and go back. He knew the caravan would not wait for a reason like bentching, so he used a reason they would accept: lost gold. This echoes בית שמאי's wallet argument (Step 23). People will go back for gold, and Heaven really did give him gold.

keyTerms.meaning: a caravan, a group traveling together

steps.whyThisMatters: The story shows that even someone who only forgot, and could rely on בית הלל, may choose to go back as an extra level of care, and it is praised.

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana
was traveling with a caravan.
He ate, forgot, and did not bentch.
He said [to himself]: What should I do?
If I tell them, "I forgot to bentch,"
they will tell me: Bentch [right here],
since wherever you bentch,
you are blessing the Merciful One.
It is better that I tell them:
I forgot a golden dove.
He said to them: Wait for me,
because I forgot a golden dove.
He went back and bentched,
and he found a golden dove.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה הֲוָה קָאָזֵל בְּשַׁיַּירְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a second story, after the two students, showing the reward for going back to bentch.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Going back to bentch where one ate, even when one only forgot, is praiseworthy and brings reward.

steps.title: Why specifically a dove?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבה בר בר חנה chose to say he forgot a dove rather than some other golden object.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is special about a dove?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question about the story: why a dove? This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on the story. It is a request to understand a detail. The גמרא assumes the choice of a dove is meaningful.

keyTerms.meaning: what is different / what is special about

phrases.english: And what is special about a dove?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי שְׁנָא יוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a detail in the story of רבה בר בר חנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the object named in the story was a dove.

steps.title: Israel is compared to a dove, saved by its wings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that כנסת ישראל is compared to a dove in תהלים. Just as a dove is saved only by its wings, the Jewish people are saved only by מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the community of Israel is compared to a dove, as it says: 'The wings of a dove covered with silver, and its feathers with shimmering gold.' Just as a dove is saved only by its wings, so too Israel is saved only by מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the dove stands for the Jewish people, who are protected by doing מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dove fits the story. רבה בר בר חנה went back to do a מצוה (bentching), and the dove hints that מצוות are what save the Jewish people, the way wings save a dove. The gold in the פסוק also matches the golden dove he found.
steps.whatToRemember: Going back to bentch is praised and rewarded. The golden dove teaches that the Jewish people are protected through מצוות, just as a dove is protected by its wings.

phrases.english: Because the community of Israel is compared to a dove.
As it is written:
"The wings of a dove covered with silver,
phrases.notes: תהלים סח:יד

phrases.english: and its feathers with shimmering gold."

phrases.aramaic: — מָה יוֹנָה אֵינָהּ נִיצּוֹלֶת אֶלָּא בִּכְנָפֶיהָ,
phrases.english: Just as a dove is saved only by its wings,

phrases.aramaic: אַף יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינָן נִיצּוֹלִין אֶלָּא בְּמִצְוֹת.
phrases.english: so too, Israel is saved only by the מצוות.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּמְתִילִי כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְיוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of why a dove.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A dove represents the Jewish people, who are saved through מצוות just as a dove is saved by its wings.

steps.title: Quoting the next phrase of the משנה: until when
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: 'Until when may he bentch?' This begins a new topic.
steps.simpleTranslation: [We learned in the משנה:] Until when does he [still bentch]? And so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is moving on. It quotes the next part of the משנה to set up a new discussion about how long after eating one can still bentch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic of where to bentch is finished. Now the focus shifts to time: the משנה says one may bentch until the food is digested, and the גמרא will explain what that means.

keyTerms.meaning: until when, up to what time
etc.: the quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: Until when does he [bentch]? Etc.
phrases.notes: The משנה continues: until the food is digested in his stomach.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד אֵימָתַי הוּא וְכוּ׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the discussion of returning to bentch and opens the next line of the משנה about the time limit for bentching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduces the משנה's time limit for bentching: until the food is digested.

steps.title: How long does digestion last?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact length of time called 'digestion', which is the deadline for bentching according to the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: How long is the time of digestion?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה said one may bentch until the food is digested. Now the גמרא asks how long that actually is, and sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave a deadline but no measurement. 'Digestion' is an inner process nobody can see, so we need a practical sign that tells a person when the time is up.

phrases.english: How long is the measure of digestion?
phrases.notes: Asks for a practical measure of the משנה's deadline 'until the food is digested'.

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּמָּה שִׁיעוּר עִכּוּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the משנה's phrase quoted in step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical length of time of 'digestion', after which one can no longer bentch.

steps.title: Not hungry again, or still thirsty from the meal
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says digestion lasts as long as a person is not hungry again. ריש לקיש says it lasts as long as he is still thirsty because of what he ate.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: As long as he is not hungry. ריש לקיש said: As long as he is thirsty because of his eating.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים each give a sign for how long digestion lasts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's sign is hunger: once you feel hungry again, the food is considered digested. ריש לקיש's sign is thirst from the meal: once that thirst is gone, the food is considered digested. Each one gives a feeling a person can notice in himself.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
As long as he is not hungry.
phrases.notes: Once he is hungry again, the time for bentching is over.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said:
As long as he is thirsty because of his eating.
phrases.notes: The thirst that comes from the food he ate.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כׇּל זְמַן שֶׁאֵינוֹ רָעֵב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29 with two opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יוחנן: until he is hungry again. ריש לקיש: as long as he is still thirsty from the meal.

steps.title: ריש לקיש is quoted elsewhere as saying four מיל
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר asks מר זוטרא how ריש לקיש could say 'thirst', since רב אמי quoted ריש לקיש as saying digestion lasts as long as it takes to walk four מיל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר בר שלמיא (some say רב יימר בר שיזבי) said to מר זוטרא: Did ריש לקיש really say this? But רב אמי said in the name of ריש לקיש: How long is digestion? The time it takes to walk four מיל!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that ריש לקיש seems to contradict himself, because two different measures are quoted in his name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One report says ריש לקיש measures by a feeling (thirst). Another report says he measures by a set time (walking four מיל, roughly 72 minutes). The same person cannot hold two different measures, so one report seems to be wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Four מיל, a set walking distance

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not against רבי יוחנן. It only asks about ריש לקיש, who seems to be quoted with two different measures.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר בַּר שֶׁלֶמְיָא לְמָר זוּטְרָא
phrases.english: Rav Yeimar bar Shelamya said to Mar Zutra,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב יֵימַר בַּר שֵׁיזְבִי לְמָר זוּטְרָא:
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Yeimar bar Sheizevi who said to Mar Zutra:
Did Reish Lakish really say this?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַב אַמֵּי אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ:
phrases.english: But didn't Rav Ami say in the name of Reish Lakish:
How long is the measure of digestion?
The time it takes to walk four mil!
phrases.notes: A fixed amount of time, not a feeling.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ הָכִי? וְהָאָמַר רַב אַמֵּי אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges ריש לקיש's opinion from step 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's measure of 'as long as he is thirsty from his eating'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Contradiction between two reports of ריש לקיש's view: thirst versus walking four מיל.

steps.title: A big meal versus a small meal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that there is no contradiction. Four מיל applies to a large meal, and thirst applies to a small meal.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here it is talking about a large meal, and here it is talking about a small meal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by saying that each quote of ריש לקיש is about a different kind of meal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A big meal takes longer to digest, so ריש לקיש gives a fixed, longer measure of walking four מיל. After a small meal, digestion depends on whether he is still thirsty from the food. Both quotes are correct, each in its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
Here... here (each source is about a different case)

steps.whatToRemember: How long one may bentch after eating depends on the meal. רבי יוחנן says until he is hungry again. ריש לקיש says four מיל for a big meal, and as long as he is thirsty from the food for a small meal.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
here, with a large meal,
phrases.notes: This is the four-מיל statement.

phrases.english: here, with a small meal.
phrases.notes: This is the thirst statement.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן בַּאֲכִילָה מְרוּבָּה, כָּאן בַּאֲכִילָה מוּעֶטֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (כאן... כאן): each statement applies to a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two reports of ריש לקיש seemed to give one general rule each, so they clashed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Four מיל is for a large meal; thirst is for a small meal. ריש לקיש is consistent.

steps.title: The next line of the משנה: wine came to them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, about wine brought to the diners after the meal, to begin discussing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Wine came to them,' etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new part of the משנה. It is setting up the next discussion about wine served after the meal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The digestion topic is now finished. The word וכו' means 'and so on', telling us to remember the rest of the משנה's line, which discusses the dispute about wine served after the meal and answering אמן.

keyTerms.meaning: Wine came to them (was brought to the diners)
Etc., and so on (the rest of the quote)

phrases.english: Wine came to them, etc.
phrases.notes: Quotes the beginning of the next line in the משנה.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּא לָהֶן יַיִן וְכוּ׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the digestion discussion and opens a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Quotes the משנה's case of wine brought after the meal as the next topic to study.

steps.title: How can someone fulfill his obligation without hearing the whole blessing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from the משנה that one may answer אמן to a Jew's blessing even without hearing all of it. It then asks how such a person could fulfill his obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that after a Jew's blessing, a person answers אמן even if he did not hear the whole blessing? But if he did not hear it, how does he fulfill his obligation?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה says we answer אמן after a Jew's blessing, and we wait to hear the whole blessing only after a כותי. The גמרא notices that this suggests a Jew's blessing does not need to be fully heard, and it challenges that idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה requires hearing the whole blessing only for a כותי. That suggests that for a Jew, hearing part of it is enough to answer אמן. But someone who wants to fulfill his obligation through another person's blessing has to hear all of it, so the גמרא asks how this can work.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? An opening for an inference the גמרא is about to question
How does he fulfill his obligation?

phrases.english: Is that to say that for a Jew
phrases.notes: This refers to the משנה's line about answering אמן after a Jew who says a blessing.

phrases.english: even though he did not hear
the whole blessing, he answers (אמן)?
But if he did not hear it, how does he fulfill (his obligation)?
phrases.notes: This is the heart of the challenge.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא שָׁמַע כּוּלָּהּ בְּרָכָה עוֹנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next part of the משנה, which discusses answering אמן after a Jew versus a כותי.
steps.kashyaTarget: The implied ruling in the משנה that a Jew's blessing need not be heard in full before one answers אמן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person cannot fulfill his obligation through a blessing he did not fully hear, so the implied leniency seems impossible.

steps.title: The case is someone who did not eat with the group
steps.stepSummary: חייא בר רב explains that the משנה is talking about a person who did not eat with the diners. רבה בר אבוה, quoted by רב נחמן, says the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: חייא בר רב said: This is a case where he did not eat with them. And רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: This is a case where he did not eat with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is that the listener is not trying to fulfill any obligation, because he did not eat with the group. He is only answering אמן to a blessing he heard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hearing the whole blessing matters only for someone who needs to fulfill his obligation through it. A person who did not eat has nothing to fulfill, so he may answer אמן even after hearing just part of it. A second אמורא gives the same explanation, which strengthens it.

keyTerms.meaning: In a case where he did not eat with them
And so said, introducing a second scholar who agrees

steps.whyThisMatters: It separates two different acts: answering אמן as a response, and answering אמן to fulfill an obligation. Only the second requires hearing the whole blessing.

phrases.english: Hiyya bar Rav said:
(The case is) where he did not eat with them,
phrases.notes: So he is not trying to fulfill any obligation.

phrases.english: And so said Rav Nachman,
in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh:
(The case is) where he did not eat with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר חִיָּיא בַּר רַב: בְּשֶׁלֹּא אָכַל עִמָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 34 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The listener was assumed to be fulfilling his obligation through the blessing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The listener did not eat, so his אמן is only a response, and full hearing is not required.

steps.title: רב and רב הונא tell their sons to grab the chance to bless
steps.stepSummary: רב told his son חייא to seize the opportunity and lead the blessing. רב הונא gave his son רבה the same advice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to his son חייא: My son, grab (the cup) and bless. And similarly, רב הונא said to his son רבה: Grab and bless.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports advice from two great fathers: when there is a chance to lead the blessing, take it quickly. This sets up the next question, about which is better.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sons are being taught that leading the blessing is something to grab rather than leave to someone else. The advice suggests that the one who blesses is better off than the one who only answers אמן. The very next step challenges that implication.

phrases.english: Rav said to Hiyya his son:
My son, grab and bless.
phrases.notes: Take the cup quickly and lead the blessing.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אֲמַר רַב הוּנָא לְרַבָּה בְּרֵיהּ:
phrases.english: And similarly Rav Huna said to Rabbah his son:
Grab and bless.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב לְחִיָּיא בְּרֵיהּ: בְּרִי, חֲטוֹף וּבָרֵיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from answering אמן to the value of being the one who leads the blessing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the opportunity comes, one should hurry to be the one who recites the blessing.

steps.title: Is blessing really greater than answering אמן?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that leading the blessing is better. It cites רבי יוסי, who taught that the one who answers אמן is greater than the one who blesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that the one who blesses is better than the one who answers אמן? But it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי יוסי says, the one who answers אמן is greater than the one who blesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the advice of רב and רב הונא to mean that blessing is better, and then attacks that idea with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The advice to grab the blessing implies that blessing is the greater act. רבי יוסי says the opposite: answering אמן is greater. So the advice seems to contradict the ברייתא. Step 39 answers this challenge.

phrases.english: Is that to say that the one who blesses is better
phrases.notes: This is inferred from 'grab and bless'.

phrases.english: than the one who answers 'אמן'?
But it was taught: Rabbi Yosei says:
Greater is the one who answers 'אמן'
than the one who blesses.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דִּמְבָרֵךְ עֲדִיף מִמַּאן דְּעָנֵי אָמֵן? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges what step 36 implies.
steps.kashyaTarget: The implication of 'grab and bless' that blessing is better than answering אמן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא from רבי יוסי says explicitly that answering אמן is greater, which contradicts that implication.

steps.title: רבי נהוראי supports רבי יוסי with a battle comparison
steps.stepSummary: Still inside the ברייתא, רבי נהוראי swears that רבי יוסי is right. He compares the one who blesses to the assistants who start a battle, and the one who answers אמן to the warriors who win it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי נהוראי said to him: By Heaven, it is so! Know that this is true: the assistants go down and start the battle, but the mighty warriors go down and win it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with רבי נהוראי, who strongly backs up רבי יוסי's teaching and gives a comparison to prove it. This makes the challenge against 'grab and bless' even stronger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one who blesses is like the assistants who open the fight. The one who answers אמן is like the warriors who come after them and finish it with victory. Since the one who finishes is greater, answering אמן is greater, which sharpens the question from step 37.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (that this is so), introducing a proof
Army assistants or lower soldiers who open the battle

steps.confusionAlert: רבי נהוראי is not answering the גמרא's question. He is still part of the ברייתא, supporting רבי יוסי, so he only strengthens the challenge against 'grab and bless'. The next step answers it.
steps.whatToRemember: Answering אמן without hearing the whole blessing works only for someone who is not fulfilling an obligation. The ברייתא holds that answering אמן is greater than blessing, which seems to clash with the advice to grab the blessing.

phrases.english: Rabbi Nehorai said to him:
phrases.notes: This is still part of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: By Heaven, it is so!
phrases.notes: An oath expressing strong agreement.

phrases.english: Know (that it is true): for the assistants go down
and start the battle,
phrases.notes: They are like the one who blesses.

phrases.english: and the mighty warriors go down and win!
phrases.notes: They are like the one who answers אמן.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי נְהוֹרַאי: הַשָּׁמַיִם, כֵּן הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא cited in step 37, reinforcing רבי יוסי's view.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוסי's teaching that the one who answers אמן is greater than the one who blesses
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי נהוראי's comparison: assistants start the battle, warriors win it

steps.title: It Is a Dispute Among תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge from רבי יוסי. Whether the one who blesses or the one who answers אמן is greater is a dispute among תנאים. A ברייתא holds that the one who blesses is rewarded first.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a dispute of תנאים. As a ברייתא teaches: both the one who blesses and the one who answers אמן are included in the verse, but they hurry to reward the one who blesses more than the one who answers אמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 37. It says רב's advice simply follows a different תנא than רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem was that רב told his son to lead the blessing, while רבי יוסי said the answerer is greater. The גמרא does not force them to agree. It shows that another ברייתא holds the one who blesses gets his reward sooner, and רב follows that view.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a dispute among the תנאים (the sages of the משנה era)
included in the meaning (of the verse)
they hurry (here: to give the reward)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two views. רבי יוסי says the one who answers אמן is greater. The other ברייתא says the one who blesses is rewarded first, and רב's advice follows it.

phrases.english: It is a dispute of Tannaim.
phrases.notes: So רב can follow the other opinion.

phrases.english: As it was taught in a baraita:
Both the one who blesses and the one who answers 'amen' are included in the meaning,
phrases.notes: Included in the verse 'stand up and bless' (נחמיה ט:ה).

phrases.english: except that they hurry to reward the one who blesses
more than the one who answers amen.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּאֵי הִיא. דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Steps 37 and 38 by showing that רב's advice follows a different תנא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute among תנאים: רב follows a different תנא than רבי יוסי.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's advice seemed to go against the accepted ברייתא of רבי יוסי.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב follows the ברייתא in which the one who blesses is rewarded first.

steps.title: שמואל Asks About Answering אמן to Schoolchildren
steps.stepSummary: שמואל asks רב whether one should answer אמן after the blessings of young schoolchildren.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל asked רב: What is the law about answering אמן after schoolchildren?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. שמואל asks רב a practical question about answering אמן after children's blessings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now we discussed how great answering אמן is. Now the question is whether every blessing earns an אמן. Children in school often say blessings just to learn them, so it is unclear whether those count.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked of him (formal question to a teacher)

phrases.english: Shmuel asked of Rav:
What is the law about answering 'amen'
after schoolchildren?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל מֵרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new practical question about answering אמן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether one answers אמן to a blessing a child says while learning in school.

steps.title: רב: Not After Children Who Are Practicing
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that one answers אמן after everyone except schoolchildren, because they are only saying the blessing to learn it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to him: We answer אמן after everyone, except schoolchildren, since they are only practicing.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers שמואל's question. One does not answer אמן to children who are just practicing a blessing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason is not that children don't count. It is that a practice blessing is not a real blessing of thanks, so there is nothing to answer אמן to.

keyTerms.meaning: they are doing it to learn (practice)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַחַר הַכֹּל עוֹנִין אָמֵן,
phrases.english: He said to him: After everyone we answer amen,
except for schoolchildren,
since they are doing it in order to learn.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַחַר הַכֹּל עוֹנִין אָמֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers שמואל's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Answer אמן after everyone except schoolchildren, because they are only practicing.

steps.title: When Children Bless for Real, We Answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits רב's rule. It applies only when the children are practicing. When they say the blessing to fulfill their obligation, one does answer אמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies when it is not the time for them to fulfill their obligation. But when they are fulfilling their obligation, we answer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to רב's rule. It explains exactly when we do not answer אמן to children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deciding factor is what the child is doing, not his age. During a lesson the blessing is practice, so no אמן is said. When the child is really blessing, such as before eating, we answer אמן like for anyone else.

keyTerms.meaning: the time of fulfilling their obligation

steps.confusionAlert: Don't conclude that we never answer אמן to children. We skip it only when they are practicing in class.
steps.whatToRemember: No אמן after a child's practice blessing. Yes אמן after a child's real blessing.

phrases.english: And this applies when it is not the time of fulfilling their obligation,
but at the time of fulfilling their obligation, we answer.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רב's rule from Step 41.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One answers אמן to children when they are blessing to fulfill their obligation, not when they are practicing.

steps.title: Does Lacking Oil Hold Back the Blessing?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא records a dispute. רבי זילאי says lacking oil for the hands holds back ברכת המזון. רבי זיואי says it does not. רב אחא says only fine oil holds it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Oil holds back the blessing, says רבי זילאי. רבי זיואי says: It does not hold it back. רב אחא says: Fine oil holds it back.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins with a ברייתא. Should one wait to rub oil on the hands after eating before saying ברכת המזון?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In those days people rubbed oil on their hands after a meal to clean them. The question is whether this is required before the blessing. The answers are: yes, no, or only when fine oil is available.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Oil holds back the blessing,
phrases.notes: Without oil on the hands, one should not yet say ברכת המזון.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Zilai.
Rabbi Zivai says: It does not hold it back.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַחָא אוֹמֵר: שֶׁמֶן טוֹב מְעַכֵּב.
phrases.english: Rav Acha says: Fine oil holds it back.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שֶׁמֶן מְעַכֵּב אֶת הַבְּרָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about preparing the hands for ברכת המזון.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are three views on whether oil on the hands is required before ברכת המזון.

steps.title: רבי זוהמאי: Dirty Hands Cannot Bless
steps.stepSummary: רבי זוהמאי compares the blessing to the Temple service. A filthy person may not serve, so filthy hands may not say the blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זוהמאי says: Just as a filthy person is unfit for the Temple service, so filthy hands are unfit for the blessing.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds one more view. It compares saying the blessing to serving in the בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זוהמאי does not focus on oil itself. His point is that the hands must not be dirty. He bases it on the Temple: a filthy כהן may not do the עבודה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zuhamai says:
Just as one who is filthy is unfit for the Temple service,
so too filthy hands are unfit for the blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זוּהֲמַאי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fourth view to the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dirty hands are unfit for ברכת המזון, just as a filthy person is unfit for the Temple service.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק Prefers a Known Source
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says he does not know זילאי, זיואי or זוהמאי. He knows only a ברייתא, which he is about to quote.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: I don't know זילאי, זיואי or זוהמאי. I know only a ברייתא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק reacts to the views above and sets up the next step. He is about to quote a source he trusts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He sets aside the opinions of these less familiar names, which also sound like wordplay on 'cheap', 'shine' and 'filth'. He prefers to rely on an established teaching, which he quotes next.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲנָא לָא זִילַאי וְלָא זִיוַאי וְלָא זוּהֲמַאי יָדַעְנָא
phrases.english: I do not know Zilai, nor Zivai, nor Zuhamai,
phrases.notes: The names hint at 'cheap', 'shine' and 'filth', matching the topic of oil and dirt.

phrases.english: rather, I know a baraita.

steps.title: The Verse: Waters, Oil and the Blessing
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק quotes רב (or a ברייתא). Each part of the פסוק "והתקדשתם" matches a stage of the meal: washing before, washing after, oil, and ברכת המזון.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יהודה said in the name of רב, and some say a ברייתא taught: "And you shall sanctify yourselves" refers to the first waters. "And you shall be holy" refers to the final waters. "For holy" refers to oil. "I am ה׳ your God" refers to the blessing.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the source רב נחמן בר יצחק promised. A פסוק is read as listing, in order, the steps that lead up to ברכת המזון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Oil comes in the list right before the blessing, as one of the stages of holiness. This supports giving oil a real role in getting ready for ברכת המזון.
steps.whatToRemember: The order is: washing before the meal, washing after it, oil, then ברכת המזון.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic source for מים ראשונים and מים אחרונים, both still part of the meal today.

steps.title: הדרן: Closing פרק אלו דברים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא marks the end of פרק אלו דברים with the traditional farewell formula הדרן עלך, meaning 'we will return to you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, 'אלו דברים' (These are the matters).
steps.whatsHappening: This is not an argument or a ruling. It is the closing line that says the chapter אלו דברים is now finished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chapter is named after its opening words, 'אלו דברים שבין בית שמאי ובית הלל בסעודה' (these are the matters on which בית שמאי and בית הלל disagree about the meal). Saying הדרן עלך expresses love for the Torah we learned and a promise to come back and review it. The discussion that just ended, about washing, oil and ברכת המזון, is the last material of this chapter.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We will return to you.' The formula said when finishing a chapter of גמרא.
'These are the matters.' The name of the eighth chapter of ברכות, taken from its opening words.
A chapter of the משנה and גמרא.

steps.whatToRemember: פרק אלו דברים is now finished. It covered the meal-related disputes of בית שמאי and בית הלל and ended with the laws of washing, oil and ברכת המזון. A new chapter comes next.
steps.confusionAlert: הדרן עלך is not part of the argument and does not answer anything from the previous steps. It is only a closing formula, like a bookmark marking the end of the chapter.
